standard.title: Science Collaboration and Building on Others' Work
standard.description: examine why advances in science are often the result of collaboration or build on the work of others
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can examine how data is used to develop scientific explanations (AC9S3H01, 3-4 band). They have not yet examined the collaborative and cumulative nature of science — the idea that advances typically require multiple people, disciplines and prior discoveries.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students examine real examples of scientific advances that required collaboration across disciplines, institutions or cultures, or that built on the prior work of others — explaining why scientific knowledge advances more effectively through collective effort than individual work alone.

nodes.label: Scientific advances build on prior work
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe at least one example where a scientific advance built on the prior work of others, explaining what earlier knowledge was required and how the new discovery extended or depended on it.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe one example where a scientific discovery built on the prior work of others, identifying the earlier work and the new contribution.
nodes.typical_width: Students examine multiple examples where scientific understanding developed cumulatively — including the history of optics (Plato, Euclid, Ibn al-Haytham, Bacon) — explaining how each contribution added to or refined what came before, and why no single scientist could have made all contributions alone.
wider: Explore how understanding of light and optics developed through contributions from Plato, Euclid, Ptolemy, Ibn al-Haytham and Roger Bacon — examining how ideas from different cultures and centuries built a cumulative scientific understanding

Investigate how contemporary soil erosion management adapts and builds on First Nations Australians' fire management and agricultural practices — examining how traditional ecological knowledge informs current scientific practice
Research why European naturalists initially rejected the platypus as a faked animal and how ongoing collaborative research has continued to reveal its features and behaviours
nodes.hinge_reason: The cumulative-science concept is foundational to the H strand at Y5 — students who retain the 'eureka individual' model will be unable to meaningfully engage with Node 2's collaboration framing, and will misread H01-linked cross-strand references throughout U and I nodes.

response_modes.reason: Students tend to think of science as a series of individual 'eureka' moments rather than as a cumulative process where each advance depends on prior work. Making the dependency chain explicit — what prior knowledge was required → what new contribution was made → what it made possible for others — is the scaffold that produces genuine understanding of science as a cumulative human endeavour.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The history of optics across cultures and centuries provides a rich, elaboration-grounded direction. The First Nations land management direction shows cumulative knowledge building across generations rather than across individual scientists — broadening the concept of scientific knowledge accumulation.
success_criteria: Describes one example of a scientific advance that built on prior work
Identifies the earlier knowledge that was required and explains how the new contribution depended on it

nodes.label: Collaboration across disciplines and institutions advances science
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain why complex scientific questions often require collaboration across disciplines, institutions or countries, and describe at least one example where such collaboration produced an advance.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe one example of scientific collaboration across at least two disciplines or groups, explaining what each contributed and why collaboration was necessary.
nodes.typical_width: Students examine multiple collaboration examples — including ecologists collaborating with engineers and computer scientists for remote sensing, and geologists/hydrologists/farmers collaborating on erosion mitigation — explaining what each discipline contributes and why the question could not be answered by one discipline alone.
wider: Explore how developing erosion mitigation techniques (contour banks, strip cropping) requires collaboration across geologists, hydrologists and farmers — examining what each brings to the problem

Research how the discovery of biofluorescent mammals (flying squirrel → wombats, bilbies, echidnas) led to international scientific collaboration across fields — examining how one discovery opened a line of collaborative inquiry
Examine why international collaboration is necessary for questions about climate, ecosystems and space — exploring the scale and complexity that require distributed scientific effort

response_modes.reason: Students tend to imagine scientists as lone individuals working in isolation. Encountering collaboration at different scales — across disciplines within a project, across institutions nationally, across countries internationally — builds a more accurate and complete model of how science actually operates.

success_criteria: Describes one example of collaboration across at least two disciplines or groups
Explains what each contributor brought to the collaboration and why a single discipline could not have answered the question alone
